State technology leaders urged Congress to continue investing in state and local cybersecurity during a May hearing before the House Homeland Security Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection, warning that artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster and more sophisticated.

Officials from Florida, New York and Tennessee called for reauthorization of the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program, saying it has helped governments strengthen defenses while extending security services to smaller jurisdictions with limited resources.

“Our states are on the front lines of multiple cyber conflicts,” said Colin Ahern, New York’s director of security and intelligence. He argued that continued federal investment is essential as states face increasingly sophisticated nation-state threats.

Click the banner below to read CDW’s latest Cybersecurity Research Report.

Tennessee CIO Kristin Darby described a “dangerous imbalance between highly sophisticated attackers and severely resource-constrained defenders.” She said Tennessee has used federal grant funding to secure nearly 90,000 endpoints across local government networks, giving many communities access to cybersecurity capabilities they otherwise could not afford.

Florida CIO Warren Sponholtz said centralized cybersecurity services help governments achieve economies of scale while expanding access to enterprise-grade protections. He also warned that artificial intelligence is accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploit development, increasing the need for close collaboration among federal, state and local governments.

Although lawmakers discussed potential changes to future grant programs, witnesses broadly agreed that sustained federal support remains critical. They also emphasized the importance of continued investment in cyber workforce development, threat intelligence sharing and AI preparedness.

The hearing highlighted a growing concern among state technology leaders: As AI lowers the barriers to sophisticated cyberattacks, strong federal-state partnerships will become increasingly important to protect government systems and the public services they support.
